hypothesis: The neuron is highly selective for high-contrast, monochromatic visual patterns, specifically characterized by sharp transitions between deep blacks or dark grays and bright whites or light grays. The core activating features consist of distinct regions of luminosity—such as white markings on dark animal fur, specular highlights on glass or wet surfaces, bright silhouettes, or illuminated shapes like flames—set against dark, shadowed, or textured backgrounds. The neuron shows strong invariance to object identity (responding to dogs, primates, glassware, logos, and figures alike) and texture (ranging from organic fur to smooth metal), provided the scene is rendered in a strict grayscale palette with intense tonal polarity. The dominant colors are exclusively neutral tones of black, charcoal, silver, and white, typically set against a background of deep shadow, black void, or blurred mid-tone gray. The high-contrast feature usually occupies approximately 30–70% of the image area and is positioned centrally or slightly off-center within the frame.
